vo.text: In June 1815, Napoleon, the most famous general in the world, was back. And this time, Europe had had enough.
Napoleon had been Emperor of France. He was beaten, and sent away to a small island. He escaped, sailed back to France, and took over again. So Europe declared war on him. All of it.
Two armies were waiting for him in Belgium. A British-led army under the Duke of Wellington. And a Prussian army under Marshal Blücher, a seventy-two year old general who never, ever gave up.
Napoleon's plan: beat them one at a time, before they could join up.
On the eighteenth of June, Wellington lined up his army along a low ridge near the village of Waterloo. Most of his soldiers waited just behind the top of the ridge, out of sight of the French guns.
In front of the ridge stood farmhouses, turned into little forts. Hougoumont on one side. La Haye Sainte in the middle.
It had rained all night. Napoleon waited for the ground to dry before attacking. Until almost midday. It turned out to be a very expensive lie in.
First, the French attacked Hougoumont. All day long. They never took it.
Then French soldiers marched at the middle of the ridge. British cavalry charged them back down the slope. And then charged a bit too far.
In the afternoon, thousands of French horsemen rode up the ridge. Wellington's soldiers formed squares, like giant hedgehogs of bayonets. The horses would not charge into them.
Meanwhile, far off to the east, Blücher's Prussians were marching. Through mud. Late. But coming.
By evening, the Prussians were smashing into Napoleon's side. So Napoleon sent in his last and best soldiers, the Imperial Guard, straight up the ridge.
Wellington's soldiers rose up out of the tall corn and fired. The Guard fell back. And when the Guard fell back, the whole French army ran.
Wellington later called it the nearest run thing you ever saw in your life.
Four days later, Napoleon gave up his throne. This time he was sent to an island in the middle of the South Atlantic. No escaping from that one.
And today, to meet your Waterloo means to meet the one thing that finally beats you.
